reception.text: The reservation was signed without ceremony and passed unremarked in the national press.

political_impact.text: Its effect fell mainly on the local egg hunters and fishermen it shut out of the island.

legacy.text: Indian Key is one of the fifty-one bird reservations Roosevelt created, the seed of the national wildlife refuge system.

today.name: Pinellas National Wildlife Refuge
today.note: Established in 1951; takes in Indian, Tarpon, Mule and Jackass Keys, closed to the public, managed within the Crystal River refuge complex.

today.name: Indian Key National Wildlife Refuge
today.note: Name given in 1940; the reservation orders were revoked in 1950.

later_actions.text: President Harding enlarged the reservation to include all mangrove islands in sections 20, 27, 28, 33 and 34 by Executive Order 3502 (sometimes misprinted as 3052).
Renamed Indian Key National Wildlife Refuge by Proclamation 2416.
Interior Secretary Oscar L. Chapman revoked the 1906 and 1921 orders, about 191 acres, by Public Land Order 650.

uncertain: How title to Indian Key passed between the 1950 revocation and the 1951 Pinellas National Wildlife Refuge has not been traced.
Whether Indian Key was part of the 1955 grant of submerged lands to Pinellas County is not settled; the Trustees' minutes for the grant mention Bush or Tarpon Key but not Indian Key.
A 1964 county rededication of Indian Key and Bush Key as a bird sanctuary rests on a single secondary article.

reception.text: A search of California papers for January through March 1906 found no coverage of the amendment.

political_impact.text: It widened a rule already resented by postal unions and other employee groups, part of a longer fight over federal workers' right to petition Congress.

legacy.text: The fight over employees' right to petition Congress was settled by the Lloyd–La Follette Act of 1912 and reshaped by later law.

related.note: Adds "or independent Government establishments" after "departments" in the 1902 gag order.
Extended to independent Government establishments in January 1906.

reception.text: An Associated Press dispatch headed "Crusade Against Consumption" reported the order briefly and neutrally; no protest over its naming and dismissal rules has been found.

legacy.text: The order is an early marker in the federal government's history as an occupational-health authority.

related.note: Puts into effect the plan of the committee appointed by the order of December 7, 1905.
The February 1906 order that put the committee's tuberculosis rules into effect.

political_impact.text: The commission was the federal government's machinery behind the Jamestown Exposition at Norfolk, which Roosevelt opened in person on April 26, 1907, and which closed on November 30, 1907.

related.note: The 1905 proclamation of the Jamestown celebration.

legacy.text: The board, renamed the United States Geographic Board in 1906, was abolished in 1934; a departmental Board on Geographic Names carried on from 1935, and Congress put the board on a statutory footing in 1947.

today.name: U.S. Board on Geographic Names
today.note: Statutory board in the Interior Department, staffed by the Geological Survey.

related.note: Renamed the board the United States Geographic Board and added advisory powers over mapmaking.

legacy.text: Fish and Wildlife Service histories credit Roosevelt with "55 bird and game reservations"; the National Park Service breaks this into fifty-one bird reserves and four national game preserves.
legacy.source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; National Park Service
